skill_title: Define reaction rate, apply collision theory, and explain factors affecting rate
notes: 20 items: 4 lifted-style, 16 fresh. Reaction rate definition, collision theory (frequency, energy, orientation), factors: concentration, surface area, temperature, catalyst, pressure (gases).

items.question: Define REACTION RATE.
items.expectedAnswer: The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
items.explanation: Rate = Δ[species]/Δt. Reactants: negative sign (consumed). Products: positive (formed). Always reported as positive.
options: The total amount of product formed in a reaction.
The change in concentration of a reactant or product per unit time.
The time taken to reach equilibrium.

items.question: State COLLISION THEORY of reaction rates.
items.expectedAnswer: Particles must collide with sufficient energy (≥ Ea) AND the correct orientation.
items.explanation: Three requirements: collision (frequency) + sufficient energy (≥ Ea) + correct orientation. Effective collisions ⇒ reaction.
options: Particles react whenever they collide, regardless of energy or orientation.
Reactions occur when particles are heated, without any collisions.
Particles must collide with sufficient energy (≥ Ea) AND the correct orientation.

items.question: How does INCREASING THE CONCENTRATION of reactants affect the reaction rate? Explain using collision theory.
items.expectedAnswer: Increases the rate — more particles per volume means more frequent collisions.
items.explanation: More particles → more collisions → more effective collisions per second → higher rate.
options: Increases the rate — more particles per volume means more frequent collisions.
Decreases the rate — crowded particles collide less.
No effect — concentration doesn't influence the rate.

items.question: How does INCREASING the SURFACE AREA of a solid reactant affect the reaction rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increases the rate — more exposed particles means more frequent collisions.
items.explanation: Powder > granules > lump. More surface area means more collision sites.
options: Decreases the rate — more surface slows contact.
Increases the rate — more exposed particles means more frequent collisions.
No effect — surface area is irrelevant to rate.

items.question: How does INCREASING the TEMPERATURE affect the reaction rate? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Increases the rate — particles have more energy and a larger fraction exceed Ea.
items.explanation: T ↑ → both frequency ↑ AND fraction with KE ≥ Ea ↑. Rate goes up sharply.
options: Decreases the rate — heat disperses the particles.
Increases the rate only by raising the activation energy.
Increases the rate — particles have more energy and a larger fraction exceed Ea.

items.question: What is the role of a CATALYST in a reaction? How does it affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing the rate.
items.explanation: Catalyst: alternative pathway, lower Ea, faster rate. Doesn't change equilibrium or ΔH.
options: It provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, increasing the rate.
It increases the activation energy, slowing the reaction.
It increases the kinetic energy of the particles.

items.question: How does INCREASING the PRESSURE of a GASEOUS reaction affect the rate?
items.expectedAnswer: Increases the rate — compressing the gas raises the concentration, so more collisions.
items.explanation: Pressure ↑ ⇒ effective [gas] ↑ ⇒ more collisions ⇒ faster.
options: Decreases the rate — higher pressure separates gas particles.
Increases the rate — compressing the gas raises the concentration, so more collisions.
No effect on gaseous reaction rates.

items.question: What is ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea)?
items.expectedAnswer: The minimum kinetic energy colliding particles need for an effective (successful) collision.
items.explanation: Ea: minimum energy for reaction. Sets the 'threshold' for effective collisions.
options: The energy released when products form.
The average kinetic energy of all the particles.
The minimum kinetic energy colliding particles need for an effective (successful) collision.

items.question: A learner says: 'A catalyst increases the kinetic energy of the reactant particles.' Is this correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Incorrect — a catalyst lowers Ea; it doesn't change the particles' kinetic energy.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea, doesn't raise KE. Common misconception.
options: Incorrect — a catalyst lowers Ea; it doesn't change the particles' kinetic energy.
Correct — a catalyst raises the particles' kinetic energy.
Correct — a catalyst increases the system's temperature.

items.question: Why does breaking a solid into smaller pieces speed up its reaction with a liquid?
items.expectedAnswer: It increases the surface area exposed, so there are more collisions per second.
items.explanation: Powder = much more surface area than lump. More reactive surface = faster reaction.
options: Because smaller pieces have a higher activation energy.
It increases the surface area exposed, so there are more collisions per second.
Because smaller pieces are at a higher temperature.

items.question: A reaction takes 200 s at 25°C. At 35°C the same reaction (same amounts) takes about 100 s. Explain why.
items.expectedAnswer: At higher T more particles exceed Ea, so a greater fraction of collisions are effective.
items.explanation: T ↑ ⇒ exponentially more particles cross Ea ⇒ rate ↑. ~10°C ≈ ×2 rule.
options: Higher temperature lowers the activation energy.
Higher temperature increases the amount of reactant.
At higher T more particles exceed Ea, so a greater fraction of collisions are effective.

items.question: What does the term EFFECTIVE COLLISION mean?
items.expectedAnswer: A collision that leads to a reaction (KE ≥ Ea and correct orientation).
items.explanation: Effective collision = enough energy AND correct orientation. Most collisions are ineffective.
options: A collision that leads to a reaction (KE ≥ Ea and correct orientation).
Any collision between two particles.
A collision that bounces particles apart without reacting.

items.question: A reaction: 2HCl(aq) + Mg(s) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). Predict the EFFECT on the rate of (a) doubling [HCl]; (b) using Mg powder instead of a strip; (c) heating the system.
items.expectedAnswer: (a) doubling [HCl] → faster; (b) Mg powder → much faster; (c) heating → faster.
items.explanation: Three factors: concentration, surface area, temperature. All increase rate when increased.
options: (a) faster; (b) slower (powder reacts less); (c) faster.
(a) doubling [HCl] → faster; (b) Mg powder → much faster; (c) heating → faster.
(a) no change; (b) faster; (c) slower.

items.question: A learner says: 'Doubling the concentration of a reactant always doubles the rate.' Is this strictly correct?
items.expectedAnswer: Not strictly — it depends on the reaction order with respect to that reactant.
items.explanation: Rate ∝ [reactant]ⁿ. n = 1: doubles. n = 2: quadruples. n = 0: unchanged.
options: Correct — rate is always directly proportional to concentration.
Incorrect — concentration never affects the rate.
Not strictly — it depends on the reaction order with respect to that reactant.

items.question: Two reactions with the same Ea proceed at different temperatures: 25°C and 45°C. At which temperature do MORE particles have KE ≥ Ea? Why?
items.expectedAnswer: At 45 °C — higher temperature shifts the energy distribution so more particles exceed Ea.
items.explanation: T ↑: distribution shifts right, more particles past Ea ⇒ more effective collisions.
options: At 45 °C — higher temperature shifts the energy distribution so more particles exceed Ea.
At 25 °C — lower temperature concentrates the energy.
Equal — temperature doesn't affect the energy distribution.

items.question: Sketch (or describe) the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at two temperatures (T₁ < T₂) and indicate the activation energy Ea.
items.expectedAnswer: At higher T₂ the curve is broader and shifted right, so more particles lie beyond Ea.
items.explanation: Maxwell-Boltzmann: shifts right and broadens at higher T. Fraction past Ea increases.
options: At higher T₂ the curve shifts left, with fewer particles above Ea.
At higher T₂ the curve is broader and shifted right, so more particles lie beyond Ea.
Both curves are identical; only Ea moves.

items.question: Explain WHY a CATALYST does NOT change the EQUILIBRIUM position.
items.expectedAnswer: It lowers Ea of the forward AND reverse reactions equally, so both rates rise the same.
items.explanation: Catalyst lowers Ea equally on both sides. Same Kc, same equilibrium position, just faster to get there.
options: Because it only speeds up the forward reaction.
Because it increases the yield of products.
It lowers Ea of the forward AND reverse reactions equally, so both rates rise the same.

items.question: Which of the following will NOT affect the reaction rate?
options: Increasing the temperature
Adding a catalyst
Increasing the concentration of a reactant
Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.expectedAnswer: Adding more of an inert gas at constant volume (gas-phase reaction)
items.explanation: Inert gas at constant V doesn't change partial pressure/concentration of reactants. No effect on rate.

items.question: Why does combustion of paper burn faster when the paper is shredded vs. as a single sheet?
items.expectedAnswer: Shredding greatly increases the surface area exposed to oxygen, so it burns faster.
items.explanation: Surface area effect again. Powders/finely divided solids react MUCH faster than bulk.
options: Shredding greatly increases the surface area exposed to oxygen, so it burns faster.
Because shredded paper has a lower activation energy.
Because shredded paper contains more fuel.

items.question: List THREE factors that can be changed to INCREASE the rate of a reaction.
items.expectedAnswer: Increase concentration (or pressure), increase temperature, increase surface area.
items.explanation: Five typical factors. CAPS expects four main ones (concentration, T, surface area, catalyst).
options: Decrease temperature, decrease concentration, decrease surface area.
Increase concentration (or pressure), increase temperature, increase surface area.
Add more product, increase the volume, cool the system.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COLLISION_THEORY_INCOMPLETE: Misses orientation or Ea in collision theory
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_CONCENTRATION: Wrong direction of concentration effect on rate
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_COLLISION_FREQUENCY: Doesn't link concentration to collision frequency
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_SURFACE_AREA: Wrong direction of surface area effect
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_T_VS_EA: Doesn't link temperature to fraction past Ea
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_RATE_PRESSURE: Wrong direction of pressure effect on gas rate
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EFFECTIVE_COLLISION: Wrong definition of effective collision (orientation + energy)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_REACTION_ORDER: Confuses qualitative rate increase with linear/quadratic order
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_MAXWELL_BOLTZMANN: Wrong description of M-B distribution shift with T
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INERT_GAS_RATE: Wrong effect of inert gas on rate
